stops.name: Toulouse, the doctorate and the chair on the soul
stops.campa: He crosses into Catholic France, to Toulouse, and there, license and past unmentioned, takes a doctorate in theology and wins by competition the ordinary lectureship in philosophy. For very nearly two years he lectures publicly on Aristotle's De Anima, the treatise on the soul, teaching within the letter of the school while privately already doubting its walls: an earth that does not move, a heaven of crystal spheres, a cosmos closed like a shell around a single sun. Students crowd to hear a lecturer whose memory needs no text before him.

stops.name: Toulouse, the wars of religion close the schools
stops.campa: In the summer, the truce between Catholic Toulouse and its Huguenot countryside breaks again into open war, as it has broken and mended a dozen times in this generation; the university empties, lecture halls stand idle, and the philosopher without a party in either camp judges it time to move again. He turns north to Paris, city of a king who has already heard, by report, of an Italian doctor whose memory performs like a conjuring trick and whose lectures on the sphere leave the schoolmen uneasy.

stops.name: Paris, the reputation that reaches Henri III
stops.campa: Paris receives the wandering Nolan into a court fascinated by exactly his kind of gift: Henri III himself, a king who collects magi, cabalists, and memory-artists the way other princes collect relics, sends for him and has him demonstrate before the whole assembled court an art of memory that lets him repeat, forward or backward, whole strings of names and words heard only once. The king asks whether the trick is natural skill or forbidden magic; Bruno answers that it is neither sorcery but a science, built on Ramon Llull's wheels and on his own reworking of them, and offers to teach it in print.
stops.quote: This memory of mine is not by magic, but by science.
stops.quote_source: Bruno's own account, given later to the Venetian inquisitors, of his reply to Henri III

stops.name: Paris, De umbris idearum laid before the king
stops.campa: From the press of Gilles Gourbin comes De umbris idearum, On the Shadows of Ideas, bound with the Ars memoriae and dedicated to His Most Christian Majesty: a book that fuses Ficino's Neoplatonic psychology, Llull's combinatorial wheels, and a hermetic doctrine of shadow-images through which the mind climbs from sense toward the intelligible sun. Bruno tells his judges afterward, plainly, what came of it: printed and dedicated to the king, the book earns him appointment as an extraordinary and paid lecturer, a post outside the ordinary faculty, since he will not attend the Mass required of a full chair.
stops.quote: After this I had a book on memory printed, under the title De Umbris Idearum, which I dedicated to his majesty; and on this occasion he made me an extraordinary and paid lecturer.

stops.name: Paris, Il Candelaio and the comedy of the age
stops.campa: The same year, Bruno lets loose Il Candelaio, The Torchbearer, a five-act comedy conceived years before in Naples and now printed at Paris: a riotous, obscene, learned satire of an alchemist, a pedant, and a lovesick miser, its Italian larded with Neapolitan slang and mock-Latin, its prologue already announcing the philosopher's contempt for a corrupt and credulous age. It is his only play, and his most Neapolitan book, written in the city of kings by a man who has not stopped being the boy from under Vesuvius.

stops.name: Paris, De compendiosa architectura and the departure for England
stops.campa: Before he leaves, Bruno prints one further book at Gourbin's press, De compendiosa architectura et complemento artis Lulli, his most direct homage to the Catalan master whose wheels he has carried since Teofilo da Vairano's rooms in Naples. Then, commended by Henri III himself with letters to his ambassador in London, Michel de Castelnau, Sieur de Mauvissière, Bruno crosses the Channel, not as a fugitive this time but as a scholar traveling under royal protection, to a Protestant island where a new and freer air is said to blow.

stops.name: London, the house of the French ambassador
stops.campa: Bruno lodges in the London house of Michel de Castelnau at Salisbury Court, guest and unofficial secretary of the French embassy, and moves for the first time in years in a circle that does not merely tolerate but courts him: the poet-courtier Philip Sidney, the translator John Florio, gentlemen curious about the new Copernican astronomy and the older Hermetic wisdom alike. Elizabeth's London, Protestant and half-Italianate, gives him the freedom to write in his own Italian rather than the schoolmen's Latin, and in this house he composes, within two years, the six dialogues that are his masterwork.

stops.name: Oxford, the disputation before the Polish prince
stops.campa: Invited to Oxford in the train of the visiting Polish Prince Albert Łaski, Bruno disputes publicly with the university doctors, defending the Copernican motion of the earth and an infinity of worlds against the fixed Aristotelian heaven the dons have taught for three centuries. His opponent, Doctor Underhill, and the assembled masters answer less with argument than with laughter at his accent and his gestures, and then with the graver charge of plagiarism, tracing his most exact citations to Ficino's own words on love and light. He leaves Oxford scorned, and famous.
stops.quote: Pedantic, obstinate ignorance and presumption, mixed with rustic incivility.
stops.quote_source: La cena de le ceneri (1584), Bruno on the Oxford doctors

stops.name: Whitehall, the Supper on Ash Wednesday
stops.campa: On the eve of Lent, Sir Fulke Greville, in chambers near Whitehall, gathers Bruno with two Oxford doctors, Torquato and Nundinio, the translator Florio, and a company of gentlemen for a supper that becomes the frame of Bruno's own account: through darkened streets without torches, across a filthy Thames-side path, to a table where the Copernican universe is argued over wine while the Oxford men, in Bruno's telling, answer with pedantry and bad Latin rather than reasoned philosophy. He will make of this single evening the setting for his first and greatest Italian dialogue.
stops.quote: Time is the father of truth, its mother is our mind.

stops.name: London, La Cena de le Ceneri and De la causa printed
stops.campa: Bruno publishes La Cena de le Ceneri, the Ash Wednesday Supper, dedicated to Castelnau, the first of the Italian dialogues, in which the earth turns, the sun is a star among others, and the Oxford doctors' Latin pedantry stands condemned beside the new cosmology. Within months follows De la causa, principio et uno, On Cause, Principle and Unity, in which the created world and its infinite divine cause are declared, against the schools, one same substance seen from within and from without: the universe is an animal, and God its indwelling soul, not a carpenter standing outside his work.
stops.quote: The universe is one, infinite, immobile.
stops.quote_source: De la causa, principio et uno, dialogue V (1584)

stops.name: London, De l'infinito universo e mondi and the Beast Expelled
stops.campa: The cosmology reaches its full statement in De l'infinito, universo e mondi, On the Infinite Universe and Worlds: no wall of crystal spheres bounds creation, but numberless suns burn in numberless systems across a space without edge or center, each perhaps peopled with its own worlds. In the same year comes Lo spaccio de la bestia trionfante, The Expulsion of the Triumphant Beast, an allegorical reform of the heavens in which the old vice-gods are voted out of the sky by a council of virtues, dedicated, like the Furori that will follow, to Sir Philip Sidney.
stops.quote: There are then innumerable suns, and an infinite number of earths revolve around these suns.
stops.quote_source: De l'infinito, universo e mondi, first dialogue (1584)

stops.name: London, De gli eroici furori and the parting from Sidney's England
stops.campa: The last of the London dialogues, De gli eroici furori, The Heroic Frenzies, closes the cycle: a sequence of love-sonnets read as an allegory of the soul's furious ascent toward the infinite One, dedicated once more to Philip Sidney. Within the year Castelnau is recalled to France and Bruno's protection with him; he sails back across the Channel he crossed two years before as an unknown foreigner and now leaves as the author of six Italian books that will outlast every court that heard him, though almost none of them yet grasp what he has actually said about the shape of the world.
